summary: The HTML format for RFCs relies on a Cascading Style Sheet specific to the RFC Series, which should account for accessibility and responsive design. This informational document describes the requirements for that default CSS.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7993 describes requirements for the default Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) on RFC pages. These pages use Hypertext Markup Language (HTML). The styles must support different devices, accessibility needs and printing.

subtitle: Requirements for the default style sheet used in RFC HTML publications.

tldr.problem: RFC HTML uses a series-specific CSS style sheet, and the default styles need shared requirements for accessibility, responsive layouts and printing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo specifies layout, font, printing and list requirements, then defines appearance guidance for selected classes used by RFC HTML.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7993 is an Informational document and the supplied metadata says RFC 9920 updates it.

today: RFC 7993 is an Informational document published in December 2016 and has been updated by RFC 9920. It describes requirements for the default CSS used in RFC HTML.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7992 defines the HTML format for RFCs and assigns visual styling to a CSS style sheet for the RFC Series. The RFC Editor embeds default CSS in published HTML, and readers can override it locally.

RFC 7993 sets requirements for that default style sheet. It says styling should not visibly change the natural-language content unless a requirement says otherwise, and notes that the details may change as publishing tools develop.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo sets requirements for the default CSS in RFC HTML pages. It says style rules should not change the document's words or meaning.

sections.title: Design Goal and General Requirements
sections.content:
The design goal is for RFCs to adapt to a wide variety of devices and displays, remain accessible to assisted readers and print correctly. The CSS must support the semantic HTML defined by RFC 7992.

The style sheet should follow W3C accessibility and mobile-device guidance and allow a broad range of internationalized scripts. The page header must include information described by the RFC Style Guide and the RFC streams document.
sections.plainLanguage: The page should work on different screen sizes, with assistive tools and on paper. It should also support many writing systems.

sections.title: Layout, Fonts, Printing and Lists
sections.content:
Examples, code and ASCII art use fixed-width fonts; text reflows on smaller screens and has a limited maximum width. Block quotes are indented, tables can show distinct header rows and links are clearly distinguished.

The default web font is sans-serif with broad Unicode support, while print uses a serif font. The embedded style sheet includes printer-friendly rules, and lists have ample spacing unless a compact class is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Text must fit smaller screens, and code must use fixed-width fonts. Links, tables and lists need clear formatting, and the embedded CSS must include print styles.

sections.title: How Selected CSS Classes Appear
sections.content:
The memo gives appearance requirements for classes used in RFC HTML. For example, .pilcrow appears at the end of a paragraph, artwork or source-code segment when pointed at, but not in printed output or copied text.

Compact list classes use less spacing, while classes such as .eref, .relref, .url and .xref must be clearly distinguishable as links. The .docInfo, .finalized and .rendered classes are hidden from visible content.
sections.plainLanguage: CSS classes identify things such as links, paragraph marks and compact lists. This section says which classes change appearance and how they should look.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that CSS can introduce vulnerabilities such as CSS injection attacks. It requires the CSS used for RFC pages to comply with current W3C CSS specifications to avoid or mitigate attack vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: CSS can create security vulnerabilities. The style sheet must follow current W3C CSS specifications to reduce that risk.
